name: Mueller-Weiss syndrome
aliases: spontaneous osteonecrosis of the adult navicular

reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A true osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular occurring in adults, distinct from the benign childhood Kohler disease and from a traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the tarsal navicular, with the lateral portion characteristically compressed and fragmented
Typically presents in middle-aged adults and is more common in women
Presents with chronic midfoot and hindfoot pain and, characteristically, a paradoxical hindfoot varus rather than the flatfoot expected with medial column collapse
The radiographic hallmark is lateral compression and fragmentation of the navicular, producing a flattened, comma-shaped bone
In contrast to Kohler disease, the adult navicular does not spontaneously reconstitute and tends to progress
The altered mechanics predispose to talonavicular and naviculocuneiform degenerative change
Management ranges from orthoses, offloading and activity modification to arthrodesis for advanced or refractory disease as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Mueller-Weiss syndrome is an osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular in the mature skeleton, thought to result from a combination of abnormal loading and impaired vascularity of the bone. Disordered ossification or delayed maturation of the navicular is believed to leave it mechanically vulnerable, and abnormal distribution of load across the midfoot then concentrates compressive stress on its lateral portion. The resulting subchondral insufficiency and osteonecrosis lead to lateral compression, fragmentation and a characteristic comma-shaped deformity of the navicular. As the lateral navicular collapses, the talar head is displaced and the hindfoot paradoxically drifts into varus rather than the valgus seen with typical medial column failure, and secondary degeneration of the surrounding tarsal joints follows.
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing foot radiographs to demonstrate lateral navicular compression and the comma-shaped deformity
Assessment of hindfoot alignment for paradoxical varus
Computed tomography to define fragmentation and secondary joint involvement
Magnetic resonance imaging to confirm osteonecrosis and assess adjacent joints
Evaluation for a navicular stress fracture as an alternative cause of midfoot pain
Screening for contributing factors such as inflammatory arthropathy where relevant
redFlags: Progressive navicular collapse with fixed hindfoot deformity
Established talonavicular or naviculocuneiform arthritis with persistent pain
Features suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy in a patient with peripheral neuropathy
Rapidly worsening pain or swelling prompting exclusion of infection or another destructive process
reference.prognosis: Unlike the self-limiting childhood Kohler disease, adult Mueller-Weiss disease tends to progress; conservative measures may control symptoms for a time, but many patients ultimately develop midfoot arthritis and deformity that require arthrodesis, with outcomes depending on the extent of collapse and secondary joint involvement.
pitfalls: Confusing the progressive adult disease with the benign, self-limiting childhood Kohler disease
Expecting a flatfoot and overlooking the characteristic paradoxical hindfoot varus
Mistaking the fragmentation for a simple navicular stress fracture
Delaying recognition of secondary midfoot arthritis until deformity is fixed
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Initial conservative management with custom orthoses, rigid-soled footwear and activity modification to offload the midfoot
Analgesia with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and periods of immobilisation during painful flares
Corrective arthrodesis (talonavicular, naviculocuneiform or triple fusion) for progressive collapse, restoring the medial column and correcting the paradoxical hindfoot varus
Surgical restoration of hindfoot alignment as part of reconstruction
Assess and treat contributing factors such as inflammatory arthropathy
Serial weight-bearing radiographs to monitor progression of navicular collapse and secondary midfoot arthritis
Referral to a foot and ankle orthopaedic surgeon when conservative measures fail
